***Carnival of Souls*** is a 1962 American [neo-noir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-noir "Neo-noir") [psychological horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological_horror "Psychological horror") film[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOlson201836-3) produced and directed by [Herk Harvey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herk_Harvey "Herk Harvey") in his sole directorial credit. The screenplay written by John Clifford[\[1\]](#cite_note-Clifford-1) from a story by Clifford and Harvey, and starring [Candace Hilligoss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candace_Hilligoss "Candace Hilligoss"). Its plot follows Mary Henry, a young woman whose life is disturbed after a car accident. She relocates to a new city, where she finds herself unable to assimilate with the locals, and becomes drawn to the pavilion of an abandoned carnival. Herk Harvey also appears in the film as a ghoulish stranger who stalks her throughout.[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) The film is set to an organ score by Gene Moore.

Filmed in [Lawrence, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence,_Kansas "Lawrence, Kansas"), and [Salt Lake City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_Lake_City "Salt Lake City"), *Carnival of Souls* was shot on a budget of $33,000, and Harvey employed various [guerrilla filmmaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerrilla_filmmaking "Guerrilla filmmaking") techniques to finish the production. The film is loosely based on the French short *[An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Occurrence_at_Owl_Creek_Bridge_\(film\) "An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge (film)")* (1961), an adaptation of the 1890 [story of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Occurrence_at_Owl_Creek_Bridge "An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge") by [Ambrose Bierce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambrose_Bierce "Ambrose Bierce"), and Harvey was inspired by the visual style of filmmakers such as [Ingmar Bergman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingmar_Bergman "Ingmar Bergman") and [Jean Cocteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Cocteau "Jean Cocteau").[\[5\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGodfreyGoodGoodall200917–18-5) *Carnival of Souls* was Harvey's only feature film, and did not gain widespread attention when originally released as a [double feature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_feature "Double feature") with the now mostly forgotten *[The Devil's Messenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Devil's_Messenger "The Devil's Messenger")* in 1962\.

Since the 1980s, the film has been noted by critics and film scholars for its cinematography and foreboding atmosphere.[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) The film has a large [cult following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_following "Cult following") and is occasionally screened at film and Halloween festivals.

## Plot

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Carnival_of_Souls&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")\]

*Carnival of Souls* (1962) by Herk Harvey

In [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas"), Mary Henry is riding in a car with two other young women when two men challenge them to a road race. During the race, the women's car is nudged by the boys' car and plunges off a bridge into a muddy river. Three hours after the police start dredging the water to look for them, Mary miraculously surfaces on the river bank, but cannot remember how she survived.

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/COS_01.JPG/250px-COS_01.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:COS_01.JPG)

Still frame of the car falling off the bridge.

Mary moves to [Salt Lake City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_Lake_City "Salt Lake City"), where she has been hired as a church organist. While driving near an [abandoned pavilion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saltair_\(Utah\)#Saltair_II "Saltair (Utah)") on the shores of the [Great Salt Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Salt_Lake "Great Salt Lake"), Mary begins experiencing visions of a ghoulish, pale-faced figure (referred to as "The Man" in the credits). A gas station attendant tells her the pavilion was first a bathhouse, then a dance hall, and finally a carnival before it was abandoned. In town, Mary rents a room and visits the church where she will be playing the organ. Mary takes a ride out to the pavilion at the lake with the church's minister who stops her from entering, warning that it is against the law.

Mary continues experiencing visions of The Man and also rejects the repeated advances of John, a socially awkward neighboring lodger. Mary goes to the pavilion by herself to investigate but does not find anything. Later, Mary begins experiencing terrifying interludes when she becomes invisible and inaudible to the rest of the world. During one of these episodes, Mary meets Dr. Samuels, who offers to help her while acknowledging he is not a [psychiatrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatrist "Psychiatrist"). Mary returns to the church by herself to practice the organ and finds herself shifting from a hymn to eerie music. In a [trance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trance "Trance"), she sees visions of The Man and other [ghouls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghoul "Ghoul") dancing at the pavilion. The minister, hearing the strange music, denounces it as [sacrilege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacrilege "Sacrilege") and insists that Mary resign.

That night, Mary accompanies John to a bar. Terrified of being alone with her nightmares, Mary tells John she wants his company, although he has little sympathy for her obvious distress and is only interested in sleeping with her. When they return home, John tries to convince Mary to let him stay the night; however, Mary becomes [hysterical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hysteria "Hysteria") when she sees The Man in the mirror. John leaves, believing Mary to be insane. The following morning, after moving out of the boarding house, she gets the transmission on her car checked; while doing so she believes she sees The Man and runs away in a fright, abandoning her car. She frantically runs around trying to escape town, but the locals do not acknowledge her and she only encounters more ghouls. Upon visiting Dr. Samuels once again and seeing he is also a ghoul she wakes up in her car, revealing the previous scenes to be merely a [nightmare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nightmare "Nightmare").

She is later drawn back to the pavilion, where she finds the ghouls dancing, with a ghoul version of herself paired with The Man. She tries to run away but is chased by the ghouls onto the beach, where she collapses as they close in. The following day, Dr. Samuels, the minister, and the police go to the pavilion to look for Mary. They find her footprints but note that she has otherwise vanished. Back in Kansas, the submerged car is finally pulled from the river. Mary's body is seen in the front seat alongside the other two women.

## Production

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Carnival_of_Souls&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")\]

### Development

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Carnival_of_Souls&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Development")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Saltair.jpg/250px-Saltair.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Saltair.jpg)

Harvey shot the film in and around the abandoned [Saltair Pavilion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saltair,_Utah "Saltair, Utah") in Salt Lake City, Utah

Harvey was a director and producer of [industrial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_film "Industrial film") and [educational films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Educational_film "Educational film") based in Lawrence, Kansas, where he worked for the [Centron Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centron_Corporation "Centron Corporation").[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) While returning to Kansas after shooting a Centron film in California, Harvey developed the idea for *Carnival of Souls* after driving past the abandoned [Saltair Pavilion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saltair,_Utah "Saltair, Utah") in Salt Lake City.[\[8\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrouse200335–38-8) "When I got back to Lawrence, I asked my friend and co-worker at Centron Films, John Clifford, who was a writer there, how he'd like to write a feature," Harvey recalled. "The last scene, I told him, had to be a whole bunch of ghouls dancing in that ballroom; the rest was up to him. He wrote it in three weeks."[\[9\]](#cite_note-champlin-9)

The screenplay is loosely based on the French short film *[An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Occurrence_at_Owl_Creek_Bridge_\(film\) "An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge (film)")* (1961), an adaptation of the 1890 [story of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Occurrence_at_Owl_Creek_Bridge "An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge") by [Ambrose Bierce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambrose_Bierce "Ambrose Bierce").[\[5\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGodfreyGoodGoodall200917–18-5)

### Casting

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Carnival_of_Souls&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Casting")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Carnival_of_Souls_-_Candace_Hilligoss_profile.jpg/250px-Carnival_of_Souls_-_Candace_Hilligoss_profile.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Carnival_of_Souls_-_Candace_Hilligoss_profile.jpg)

Candace Hilligoss, 1962

In New York City, Harvey discovered twenty-six-year-old actress Candace Hilligoss, who had trained with [Lee Strasberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Strasberg "Lee Strasberg"), and cast her in the lead role of Mary Henry.[\[9\]](#cite_note-champlin-9) Hilligoss had been offered a role in the Richard Hilliard-directed horror film *[Violent Midnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violent_Midnight "Violent Midnight")* (1963), but opted for the role in *Carnival of Souls*.[\[10\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeaver2003146-10) She stated that at the time, she took the role as a "take-the-money-and-run type of situation";[\[11\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeaver2003147-11) she was paid approximately $2,000 for her work in the film.[\[12\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeaver2003152-12)

### Filming

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Carnival_of_Souls&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Filming")\]

Harvey shot *Carnival of Souls* in three weeks on location in Lawrence and Salt Lake City,[\[9\]](#cite_note-champlin-9) after taking three weeks off from his job at Centron in order to direct the film,[\[8\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrouse200335–38-8) and starting with an initial production budget of $17,000.[\[8\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrouse200335–38-8) He raised the $17,000 cash budget by asking local businessmen if they were willing to invest $500 in his production.[\[13\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHillegass199618–33-13) The other $13,000 of the total $30,000 budget was deferred.[\[13\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHillegass199618–33-13) Harvey was able to secure the rental of the Saltair Pavilion for $50, and several other scenes, such as the scene featuring Mary in the department store, were shot [guerrilla style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerrilla_filmmaking "Guerrilla filmmaking"), with Harvey paying off locals to allow the crew to quickly film.[\[9\]](#cite_note-champlin-9)[\[14\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeaver2003148–149-14) Hilligoss described the filming process as brisk, with the cast and crew working seven days a week.[\[15\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeaver2003148-15)

Harvey aimed for the film to have "the look of [Bergman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingmar_Bergman "Ingmar Bergman") and the feel of [Cocteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Cocteau "Jean Cocteau"),"[\[16\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGodfreyGoodGoodall200918-16) and employed techniques he had learned in his work on industrial films in order to limit production costs.[\[8\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrouse200335–38-8) There was not enough money for a process screen to create a [rear projection effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rear_projection_effect "Rear projection effect"), which was the method typically used at that time to create the impression that a scene was taking place inside a moving car, by combining footage shot inside a static car with separate footage of a moving background.[\[8\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrouse200335–38-8) Instead, Harvey used a battery-powered hand-held [Arriflex camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arriflex_35 "Arriflex 35") to film the shots inside moving cars, removing the need for [compositing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compositing "Compositing"). The Arriflex, which was at that time more often used by cameramen filming newsreel footage, also allowed them to use a moving camera in other scenes without the need for gear like dollies or cranes.[\[8\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrouse200335–38-8)

Harvey's assistant director was [Reza Badiyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reza_Badiyi "Reza Badiyi"), a young Iranian immigrant who was just beginning his film work in the States. At this time, Badiyi had been second-unit director on one other film, [Robert Altman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman "Robert Altman")'s directing debut, *[The Delinquents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Delinquents_\(1957_film\) "The Delinquents (1957 film)")*,[\[17\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeaver201188-17) but would go on to make (amongst other notable work) some of the best-known, iconic [television series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_series "Television series") openings and montages, including *[Hawaii Five-O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_Five-O_\(1968_TV_series\) "Hawaii Five-O (1968 TV series)")*, *[Get Smart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get_Smart "Get Smart")*, and *[The Mary Tyler Moore Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mary_Tyler_Moore_Show "The Mary Tyler Moore Show")*.[\[18\]](#cite_note-18) The shot in which the face of The Man appears in the car window was accomplished through the use of an angled mirror placed on the far side of the window. The scene at the start of the film in which the car goes off the bridge and into the river was filmed in [Lecompton, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecompton,_Kansas "Lecompton, Kansas"). The town did not charge a fee for the use of the bridge, only requiring the film crew to replace the bridge's damaged rails once they were done filming. This was done, at a cost of $12 for the repair.[\[19\]](#cite_note-19)

### Musical score

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Carnival_of_Souls&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Musical score")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/COS_03.JPG/250px-COS_03.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:COS_03.JPG)

Hilligoss (as Mary Henry) playing organ.

*Carnival of Souls* features an original organ score by local Kansas City organist and composer Gene Moore. Film and music scholar Julie Brown comments on the score, noting: "The organ is one of the spectral presences in *Carnival of Souls*, summoning, or being summoned by, the various allusions in the film to cinema's past."[\[20\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown20093-20) Screenwriter John Clifford has stated that the locations Harvey chose for the film (particularly the Saltair Pavilion, and the grand [church organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organ_\(music\) "Organ (music)")) influenced the decision to use an organ score.[\[20\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown20093-20) The onscreen depiction of the organ played by Mary was implemented by Harvey to add to the film's "Gothic look."[\[21\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown20094-21)

An original soundtrack album for *Carnival of Souls* was released in 1988, featuring Gene Moore's original musical score.[\[22\]](#cite_note-22)

In 2023, Waxwork Records licensed the soundtrack rights from Peter Soby and Matthew Irvine and released *Carnival of Souls* as part of the *[Rob Zombie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Zombie "Rob Zombie") Presents* soundtrack series. It was pressed on colored vinyl and housed in special packaging featuring artwork by [Graham Humphreys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Humphreys "Graham Humphreys").[\[23\]](#cite_note-23)

## Release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Carnival_of_Souls&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Release")\]

*Carnival of Souls* had its world premiere at the Granada Theatre in Lawrence, Kansas, on September 26, 1962\.[\[24\]](#cite_note-24)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Carnival_of_Souls_film_premiere_poster.jpg/250px-Carnival_of_Souls_film_premiere_poster.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Carnival_of_Souls_film_premiere_poster.jpg)

Carnival of Souls film premiere poster

While the US release of *Carnival of Souls* failed to include a copyright on the prints, automatically placing them in the public domain,\[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*\] the foreign release marketed by Walter Manley did contain a copyright card and was protected for overseas sales. The 35 mm theatrical prints were cut by Herz-Lion to 78 minutes,[\[25\]](#cite_note-25)\[*[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")*\] which trimmed the camera original. However, the 16 mm television copies were printed complete and individually cut by each station to fit their time slot, which is why they vary in length.\[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*\]

[WOR-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WWOR-TV "WWOR-TV") in New York City used to broadcast the film intact in a late-night time slot in the 1960s. The scenes cut by the theatrical distributor include a scene where Mary stops at a gas station and discusses the carnival building with the attendant, a longer dialogue sequence between the organ factory boss and a carpenter, and an extra scene where the doctor talks to the landlady. In 1989, the film was screened at festivals across Europe and the United States, affording it renewed public interest,[\[26\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeaver2003154–155-26) and it has subsequently appeared at numerous Halloween film festivals.[\[27\]](#cite_note-niccum-27)

Prints of *Carnival of Souls* vary in length, from 78 minutes in the theatrical release to 84 minutes in the original cut. While some sources have erroneously listed the film at a 91-minute-runtime, Michael Weldon stated in *[The Psychotronic Video Guide to Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychotronic_Video "Psychotronic Video")* that the original theatrical cut of the film ran approximately 80 minutes.[\[2\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeldon199693-2) He also stated that the director's cut, which runs 84 minutes, is "the best and most complete version we'll ever see."[\[2\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeldon199693-2)

### Reception and legacy

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Carnival_of_Souls&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Reception and legacy")\]

*Carnival of Souls* went largely unnoticed by critics upon its initial release and received "delayed acclaim" in the ensuing decades,[\[9\]](#cite_note-champlin-9) with numerous arthouse screenings in 1989 in conjunction with the Halloween season.[\[28\]](#cite_note-ebert-28) It has since become regarded by many film schools as a classic, often praised for its lighting and sound design, in which "sight and sound come together... in a horrifying way."[\[29\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHawkins200015-29) Some scholars, such as [S. S. Prawer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegbert_Salomon_Prawer "Siegbert Salomon Prawer"), consider *Carnival of Souls* more an [art film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_film "Art film") than a straightforward horror film.[\[30\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHawkins200027-30) The *[Time Out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Out_\(magazine\) "Time Out (magazine)")* film guide commended the film's "striking black-and-white compositions, disorienting dream sequences and eerie atmosphere," adding that the film "has the feel of a silent [German expressionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_expressionist_cinema "German expressionist cinema") movie. Unfortunately, so does some of the acting, which suffers from exaggerated facial expressions and bizarre gesturing. But the mesmerising power of the carnival and dance-hall sequences far outweighs the corniness of the awkward intimate scenes."[\[31\]](#cite_note-time-31)

[Leonard Maltin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Maltin "Leonard Maltin") gave *Carnival of Souls* a score of two-and-a-half out of four stars, calling the film an "eerie" and "imaginative low budget effort."[\[32\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaltin2014218-32) Critic [Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") likened the film to a "lost episode of *[The Twilight Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Zone "The Twilight Zone")*," and noted that it possessed an "intriguing power."[\[28\]](#cite_note-ebert-28) Joe Brown of *[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post "The Washington Post")* remarked upon the film's cinematography, writing: "Harvey's camerawork gives a new twist to the word 'deadpan,' making the most mundane places and people imaginable seem like ghastly hallucinations, and the director shows a flair for elegantly employing existing locations and lighting for maximum disorientation value."[\[33\]](#cite_note-washintonrev-33) [Stephen Holden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Holden "Stephen Holden") of *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* saw the 1989 screening at the Fantasy Festival and wrote: "What has earned *Carnival of Souls* its reputation is the director's knack for building a mood of fatalistic angst."[\[34\]](#cite_note-34) The *[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")*' Peter Rainer perceived the film's cinematography to be inconsistent in merit, called the acting "fairly amateurish" with "a one-take-only quality", and noted the "inept [post-dubbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubbing_\(filmmaking\) "Dubbing (filmmaking)")"; however, he concluded that "these rinky-dink elements only add to the horror."[\[35\]](#cite_note-35)

*[TV Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV_Guide "TV Guide")* gave *Carnival of Souls* a score of three stars out of four, praising the film's atmosphere, acting, and eerie score, calling it, "A chilling ghost story with artistic pretensions."[\[36\]](#cite_note-TVGuide-36) *Film Reel.com* gave *Carnival of Souls* a positive review, praising the film's atmosphere, slow-building tension, and disturbing visuals.[\[37\]](#cite_note-37)

On [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), the film has an approval rating of 87% based on 67 reviews, with a rating average of 7\.2/10. The site's consensus states that the film "offers delightfully chilling proof that when it comes to telling an effective horror story, less can often be much, much more".[\[38\]](#cite_note-38)

*Carnival of Souls* has gradually developed a [cult following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_following "Cult following") since its release and is now considered a low-budget classic.[\[33\]](#cite_note-washintonrev-33)[\[28\]](#cite_note-ebert-28)[\[36\]](#cite_note-TVGuide-36) The film has since been included on multiple lists by various media outlets as one of the [greatest horror films ever made](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Films_considered_the_best "Films considered the best"). [*Complex* magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_\(magazine\) "Complex (magazine)") ranked *Carnival of Souls* number 39 on its list of the 50 scariest movies ever made.[\[39\]](#cite_note-39) *[Slant Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slant_Magazine "Slant Magazine")* placed the film at number 32 on its "100 Best Horror Movies of All Time".[\[40\]](#cite_note-slantmagazinelist-40) *[Paste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paste_\(magazine\) "Paste (magazine)")* magazine ranked the film at number 85 on its list of "100 Best Horror Movies of All Time".[\[41\]](#cite_note-vorel19-41)

### Rights

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Carnival_of_Souls&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Rights")\]

*Carnival of Souls* is in the public domain in the United States because it lacked a valid [copyright notice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_notice "Copyright notice").[\[42\]](#cite_note-42)[\[43\]](#cite_note-43) The original negative and a handful of surviving prints and outtakes, were purchased from the filmmakers, along with supposed film rights, by Peter Soby and Matthew Irvine of Chicago West Entertainment in January 1997 and created a new *Director's Cut* to copyright the next year.[\[44\]](#cite_note-44)[\[45\]](#cite_note-45) However, later Blu-Ray releases would only contain the Theatrical cut despite Criterion's insistence that the film as a whole is protected under copyright.[\[46\]](#cite_note-46)

### Home media

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Carnival_of_Souls&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Home media")\]

*Carnival of Souls* has been released in a significant number of formats through numerous distributors, which, according to film scholars Chris Vander Kaay and Kathleen Fernandez-Vander Kaay, has ensured it "a constant presence in the video market and \[contributed to\] its enduring cult popularity."[\[47\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVander_KaayFernandez-Vander_Kaay201648-47) [The Criterion Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Criterion_Collection "The Criterion Collection") licensed a remastered version of the film from Peter Soby and Matthew Irvine and issued a 2-disc [DVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD "DVD") set of the film in 2000, featuring both a 78-minute theatrical version and an extended 84-minute director's cut.[\[48\]](#cite_note-48) In 2009, [Legend Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legend_Films "Legend Films") released the film on DVD featuring both the black-and-white and a [colorized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_colorization "Film colorization") version of the directors cut, including an [audio commentary track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_commentary_\(DVD\) "Audio commentary (DVD)") by comedian [Michael J. Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_J._Nelson "Michael J. Nelson"), a former writer and host of *[Mystery Science Theater 3000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystery_Science_Theater_3000 "Mystery Science Theater 3000")*.[\[49\]](#cite_note-49) In 2016, the Criterion Collection reissued the film on DVD, as well as premiering it on [Blu-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray "Blu-ray"), featuring a new restoration.[\[50\]](#cite_note-50)

In 2012, the [Academy Film Archive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Film_Archive "Academy Film Archive") restored *Carnival of Souls* alongside Peter Soby and Matthew Irvine.[\[51\]](#cite_note-51) They also keep the original negatives stored in their facilities. The film has been named as a precursor to the works of various filmmakers, including [David Lynch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lynch "David Lynch"),[\[52\]](#cite_note-ew-52) [George A. Romero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_A._Romero "George A. Romero"),[\[53\]](#cite_note-53) [Lucrecia Martel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucrecia_Martel "Lucrecia Martel")[\[54\]](#cite_note-54) and [James Wan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Wan "James Wan").[\[52\]](#cite_note-ew-52)[\[55\]](#cite_note-55)[\[56\]](#cite_note-56)

The film was used for a [RiffTrax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RiffTrax "RiffTrax") Live event in October 2016, where former *[Mystery Science Theater 3000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystery_Science_Theater_3000 "Mystery Science Theater 3000")* cast members [Bill Corbett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Corbett "Bill Corbett"), [Kevin Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Murphy_\(actor\) "Kevin Murphy (actor)") and [Michael J. Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_J._Nelson "Michael J. Nelson")[\[57\]](#cite_note-57) riffed the film for a live audience and broadcast to other theaters through [NCM Fathom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_CineMedia "National CineMedia"). Rifftrax's website offers the video downloads of the live performance as well as a studio-recorded riff of the film.[\[58\]](#cite_note-58)

A novelization of the film titled *Nightmare Pavilion*, written by Andrew J. Rausch, was released by Happy Cloud Media in October 2020\.[\[59\]](#cite_note-59)

### Carnival of Souls (1998)

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Carnival_of_Souls&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Carnival of Souls (1998)")\]

Main article: [Carnival of Souls (1998 film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnival_of_Souls_\(1998_film\) "Carnival of Souls (1998 film)")

Producer Peter Soby negotiated the rights to the title from Herk Harvey and John Clifford, resulting in the loose 1998 remake of *Carnival of Souls* (also known as *Wes Craven Presents Carnival of Souls*). Sidney Berger, who appears in the original film as John Linden, appears in a cameo in the later film.

part.text: All five films have ~1-per-minute preview thumbnails on Archive.org. Let me download them and build reference luminance profiles.

input.command:
mkdir -p refs && cd refs
python3 - <<'EOF'
import json, urllib.request, os

ids = {
 'notld': 'night-of-the-living-dead_1968',
 'carnival': 'carnivalofsouls_201907',
 'hohh': 'house-on-haunted-hill_202409',
 'lme': 'TheLastManOnEarthHD',
 'lsh': 'the-little-shop-of-horrors-1960_202310',
}
for key, ident in ids.items():
    with urllib.request.urlopen(f'https://archive.org/metadata/{ident}') as r:
        d = json.load(r)
    thumbs = [f['name'] for f in d['files'] if '.thumbs/' in f['name'] and f['name'].endswith('.jpg')]
    with open(f'{key}_thumbs.txt','w') as fh:
        fh.write('\n'.join(thumbs))
    print(key, ident, len(thumbs))
    # print numbering pattern of first 5 and last 3
    print('  ', [t.split('_')[-1] for t in thumbs[:5]], '...', [t.split('_')[-1] for t in thumbs[-3:]])
EOF

part.text: The thumbnail filenames are keyed by seconds of video (~every 60s). Downloading all of them now:

input.command:
cd refs
python3 - <<'EOF'
import subprocess, os
ids = {
 'notld': 'night-of-the-living-dead_1968',
 'carnival': 'carnivalofsouls_201907',
 'hohh': 'house-on-haunted-hill_202409',
 'lme': 'TheLastManOnEarthHD',
 'lsh': 'the-little-shop-of-horrors-1960_202310',
}
os.makedirs('thumbs', exist_ok=True)
jobs = []
for key, ident in ids.items():
    os.makedirs(f'thumbs/{key}', exist_ok=True)
    names = open(f'{key}_thumbs.txt').read().split('\n')
    for n in names:
        fn = n.replace('/', '~')   # flat local name
        jobs.append((key, ident, n, fn))
with open('dl_list.txt','w') as fh:
    for key, ident, n, fn in jobs:
        fh.write(f'https://archive.org/download/{ident}/{n}\tthumbs/{key}/{fn}\n')
print(len(jobs), 'thumbs to download')
EOF
wc -l dl_list.txt

input.command:
cd refs
python3 - <<'EOF'
import urllib.request, os, concurrent.futures as cf

jobs = []
for line in open('dl_list.txt'):
    url, out = line.strip().split('\t')
    jobs.append((url, out))

os.makedirs('thumbs', exist_ok=True)
def get(job):
    url, out = job
    if os.path.exists(out) and os.path.getsize(out) > 1000:
        return True
    try:
        req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={'User-Agent':'Mozilla/5.0'})
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=40) as r:
            data = r.read()
        open(out,'wb').write(data)
        return True
    except Exception as e:
        return False

with cf.ThreadPoolExecutor(12) as ex:
    res = list(ex.map(get, jobs))
print('ok:', sum(res), 'failed:', len(res)-sum(res))
EOF
find thumbs -name '*.jpg' | wc -l

from PIL import Image
import numpy as np, os, json

def frame_luma(path):
    im = Image.open(path).convert('L')
    a = np.asarray(im).astype(np.float32)
    # trim uniform borders (letterbox/pillarbox): rows/cols whose std ~ 0
    rows = np.where(a.std(axis=1) > 1.0)[0]
    cols = np.where(a.std(axis=0) > 1.0)[0]
    if len(rows): a = a[rows[0]:rows[-1]+1]
    if len(cols): a = a[:, cols[0]:cols[-1]+1]
    return float(a.mean()), a.shape

refs = {}
for key in ['notld','carnival','hohh','lme','lsh']:
    d = f'thumbs/{key}'
    items = []
    for fn in os.listdir(d):
        num = fn.split('_')[-1].split('.')[0]
        t = int(num)
        luma, shape = frame_luma(os.path.join(d, fn))
        items.append((t, luma, shape, fn))
    items.sort()
    refs[key] = items
    shapes = {}
    for t, l, s, fn in items: shapes[s] = shapes.get(s,0)+1
    lum = [round(l) for t,l,s,fn in items]
    ts = [t for t,l,s,fn in items]
    print(f'== {key}: {len(items)} thumbs, shapes={shapes}')
    print('  times:', ts[:6], '...', ts[-3:])
    print('  luma :', lum)

np.save('refs_raw.npy', {k: [(t,l) for t,l,s,f in v] for k,v in refs.items()}, allow_pickle=True)
EOF

input.command:
cd refs
python3 - <<'EOF'
from PIL import Image
import numpy as np, os

# target profile
a = np.asarray(Image.open('../barcode.png').convert('RGB')).astype(np.float32)
target = a.mean(axis=(0,2)) / 255.0   # 1000 values, 0..1
TW = len(target)

def smooth(x, sigma_frac):
    # gaussian smoothing with sigma as fraction of series length
    n = len(x)
    sig = sigma_frac * n
    half = int(4*sig)
    xs = np.arange(-half, half+1)
    k = np.exp(-0.5*(xs/sig)**2); k /= k.sum()
    pad = np.concatenate([np.full(half, x[0]), x, np.full(half, x[-1])])
    return np.convolve(pad, k, mode='valid')

ts = smooth(target, 0.025)
tsz = (ts - ts.mean()) / ts.std()

refs_raw = np.load('refs_raw.npy', allow_pickle=True).item()

def build(key):
    items = sorted(refs_raw[key])
    t = np.array([i[0] for i in items], float)
    l = np.array([i[1] for i in items], float)/255.0
    # uniform grid over [0, t[-1]]
    grid = np.linspace(0, t[-1], 400)
    g = np.interp(grid, t, l)
    return t, l, g

results = []
for key in ['notld','carnival','hohh','lme','lsh']:
    t, l, g = build(key)
    gs = smooth(g, 0.025)
    gz = (gs - gs.mean()) / gs.std()
    best = None
    for lag in range(-30, 31, 2):   # up to ±7.5% shift
        shifted = np.roll(gz, lag)
        r = np.corrcoef(tsz, shifted)[0,1]
        if best is None or r > best[1]:
            best = (lag, r)
    # spearman on smoothed
    from scipy.stats import spearmanr
    bests = None
    for lag in range(-30, 31, 2):
        shifted = np.roll(gz, lag)
        rho = spearmanr(tsz, shifted).correlation
        if bests is None or rho > bests[1]:
            bests = (lag, rho)
    print(f'{key:9s} pearson r={best[1]:.3f} (lag {best[0]*0.25:+.1f}%)  spearman rho={bests[1]:.3f} (lag {bests[0]*0.25:+.1f}%)')
    results.append((best[1], key))

results.sort(reverse=True)
print('\nranking:', [(k, round(r,3)) for r,k in results])
EOF
